concepts.title: Infrastructure as Code: Declarative, Idempotent Infrastructure
concepts.description: Infrastructure as Code treats servers, networks, and cloud resources as version-controlled, machine-applied configuration rather than objects clicked into existence by hand -- the declarative, idempotent execution model used by tools like Terraform is what makes infrastructure changes reviewable, repeatable, and safe to apply more than once.
learningObjectives: Explain what 'infrastructure as code' means and why manually-configured infrastructure is hard to reproduce and audit.
Distinguish declarative IaC (describe the desired end state) from imperative scripting (describe the steps to reach it), and explain why most IaC tools favor the declarative model.
Explain idempotency and why an idempotent apply can be safely run repeatedly with no unintended side effects.
Read and reason about a plan/apply workflow, including what 'state' represents and why it must be shared across a team.
Identify the risks of manual, out-of-band changes to infrastructure managed by an IaC tool, and explain why drift undermines the model's core guarantee.

sections.heading: Why Infrastructure as Code at All? The Problem With Hand-Clicked Infra
sections.body:
Before IaC, infrastructure was commonly provisioned by hand -- clicking through a cloud console, or SSHing into a box and running commands to install and configure things. This produces what's sometimes called a 'snowflake' server: unique, undocumented, and subtly different from every other server that was supposedly configured 'the same way,' because ad hoc manual fixes accumulate over time and nobody keeps a complete, accurate record of every one of them. There's no audit trail of who changed what and why beyond whatever anyone happened to write down, disaster recovery becomes largely guesswork (rebuilding a server exactly as it was requires remembering every manual tweak made over months or years, which nobody actually does), and scaling requires repeating the same error-prone manual steps N times, with N chances for a slip.

Infrastructure as Code fixes this by expressing the desired infrastructure as text files, checked into version control, applied by tooling -- extending the exact same discipline already applied to application code: changes go through a diffable pull request, get reviewed before being applied, and leave a permanent history of who changed what and why. The infrastructure becomes something you can read, not something you have to remember or reverse-engineer from a running system.

sections.heading: Declarative vs Imperative: Describing the What, Not the How
sections.body:
An imperative approach describes a sequence of actions to reach a desired state -- a shell script that runs `create vpc`, then `create subnet`, then `launch instance`, in order. The problem is that running such a script twice is not automatically safe: without deliberate extra logic to check 'does this already exist' before every single step, a second run can error out partway through, or worse, silently create duplicate resources.

A declarative approach -- what Terraform, and most modern IaC tools, use -- instead has you describe the *desired end state*: 'there should be exactly one instance of this type, with this security group, with this tag.' The tool itself is responsible for figuring out the difference between what currently exists and what you've declared should exist, and for performing whichever create, update, or destroy actions are needed to reconcile the two. You never write the 'check if it already exists first' logic yourself -- the tool's diffing engine handles that uniformly, for every resource type, every time, which is exactly what makes declarative tools safe to run repeatedly in a way that a naive imperative script generally isn't.

sections.heading: Idempotency: Why Applying Twice Should Be a No-Op
State: What the Tool Actually Diffs Against
sections.body:
Terraform (and similar tools) keep a **state** file -- a record of what the tool believes exists, including real resource IDs and their last-known attributes, mapping each block in your configuration to an actual object in the cloud provider. A `plan` is essentially a diff between your desired configuration and this recorded state (optionally refreshed against the real infrastructure first); an `apply` performs whatever actions are needed to make reality match that diff.

This has a direct, practical consequence for teams: state needs to be stored somewhere shared and durable -- a remote backend such as an object store with locking (for example, an S3 bucket paired with a DynamoDB lock table) -- rather than as a local file on one engineer's laptop. If two engineers each hold their own local copy of state, their views of 'what currently exists' can diverge, and applying from either one can create duplicated resources or silently clobber the other's changes. Remote state with locking additionally prevents two applies from running concurrently and racing each other -- a second `apply` attempt simply waits (or fails fast) if another one currently holds the lock, rather than both proceeding and interleaving their changes unpredictably.

sections.heading: Configuration Drift: When Reality and Code Disagree
sections.body:
**Drift** happens when the real infrastructure changes outside the IaC tool's knowledge -- someone manually resizes an instance in the cloud console during an incident, or an auto-scaling event changes an attribute the tool also manages. Once that happens, the tool's recorded state (or the desired configuration) no longer matches reality, and the next `plan` will show a diff that can be genuinely surprising: it often looks like it's proposing to 'revert' the manual change, because from the tool's point of view, the configuration still says what it always said, and it's reality that has since deviated from it.

The deeper cost of drift isn't any single confusing plan output -- it's that undetected drift, repeated enough times, erodes the core guarantee IaC exists to provide: that the code is the authoritative source of truth for what infrastructure looks like. The practical fix is cultural as much as technical: treat IaC-managed resources as strictly off-limits for manual console or SSH changes -- 'if it's managed by Terraform, only Terraform touches it' -- and run `plan` regularly (or use dedicated drift-detection tooling) so that any drift that does occur is caught and deliberately reconciled -- either by updating the configuration to formally adopt the change, or by applying to force reality back to what the code says -- rather than left to linger silently until it causes a confusing incident.

examples.title: Idempotent Apply: Declarative Terraform
examples.explanation: Running `terraform apply` against this file the first time creates the bucket. Running it again, unchanged, produces a plan of '0 to add, 0 to change, 0 to destroy' -- Terraform compares this declared desired state against what it recorded in state (and, on refresh, against the real bucket) and finds them already reconciled, so it takes no action at all. This is the idempotency guarantee made concrete: nothing about the outcome depends on how many times this exact file has been applied before, only on whether the declared configuration currently matches reality.

examples.title: The Imperative Equivalent, and Why It's Not Idempotent By Default
examples.explanation: Run this command once and it launches one instance -- exactly as intended. Run the identical command a second time (for instance, because a CI step retried after a network blip) and it launches a *second*, separate instance, because the command has no built-in notion of 'the desired end state' to compare against -- it simply executes the requested action every time it's invoked. Making this idempotent would require deliberately added logic: either an existence check beforehand (query for an instance with a specific tag, only create if absent) or passing a client-side idempotency token that the API itself uses to deduplicate retried requests. A declarative tool gives you this property automatically, for every resource type, without you having to hand-write that check yourself each time.

examples.title: Detecting Drift with a Plan
examples.explanation: The `~` marks an in-place update, and the direction of the diff -- `t3.large -> t3.micro` -- often surprises people at first, because it reads as though Terraform is about to 'undo' the manual fix, which is exactly what it's proposing to do: from Terraform's perspective, the configuration has always said `t3.micro`, and it's reality that silently deviated from it. This is precisely the moment where a deliberate decision needs to be made rather than a reflexive `apply`: if the manual resize should stick, the configuration should be edited to say `t3.large` so the code becomes the accurate source of truth again; if the resize was only meant to be temporary, applying now correctly and intentionally reverts it. What must not happen is discovering this plan output weeks later, having forgotten the manual change was ever made, and applying without understanding which of those two outcomes is about to happen.

misconceptions.description: Infrastructure as code just means 'a script that sets up my servers' -- any automation script counts, whether it's an imperative bash script or declarative HCL.
misconceptions.clarification: Scripting infrastructure setup is a form of automation, but it doesn't automatically give you the specific guarantees the term 'IaC' usually implies in modern practice: state tracking, automatic diffing between desired and actual state, idempotent re-application, and drift detection. An imperative bash script that provisions resources step by step can certainly automate the *initial* setup, but running it again doesn't safely converge to the same state the way a declarative tool's apply does -- it takes deliberate, hand-written extra logic to make an imperative script behave idempotently at all. The guarantees, not merely the presence of a script, are the actual point of the practice.

misconceptions.description: Once infrastructure is defined in Terraform, it's fine to make a quick manual fix in the cloud console for something urgent, as long as you remember to update the .tf files afterward to match.
misconceptions.clarification: Drift begins the instant the manual change happens, regardless of any later intention to reconcile it -- and 'remembering to update the file afterward' is exactly the discipline IaC exists to remove the need for, precisely because it's the kind of manual bookkeeping step that reliably gets forgotten under the same time pressure that motivated the quick fix in the first place. If the file update is forgotten, the next ordinary apply can silently revert the urgent fix without anyone intending that; if the update happens but nobody documents why, the next engineer to read the config has no idea the value encodes an emergency workaround rather than a deliberate decision. The safer process, even under time pressure, is to make the emergency change through the IaC tool itself (a fast, targeted, reviewed apply), or at the very least to immediately follow up with a plan/apply cycle to reconcile state before the drift has any chance to be forgotten.

exercises.prompt: This HCL was already applied once, and the real infrastructure matches it exactly (no drift). What happens when `terraform apply` is run again, unchanged?
hints: What does Terraform's `plan` step actually compare -- the file against nothing, or the file against recorded state and real infrastructure?
If that comparison finds zero differences, is there anything left for `apply` to actually do?
Think about idempotency: what SHOULD happen, by design, if you apply the exact same declared state twice in a row with nothing having changed in between?
exercises.expectedAnswer: Nothing changes. Terraform reports something like 'No changes. Your infrastructure matches the configuration,' and performs zero create/update/destroy actions, because the plan step finds the desired configuration, the recorded state, and the real infrastructure already fully in agreement.
exercises.solutionExplanation: Terraform's plan step diffs the desired configuration against its recorded state (and, on refresh, the real infrastructure). Since nothing in the file changed and no drift occurred, that diff comes back empty -- there is nothing to add, change, or destroy. This is idempotency working exactly as intended: applying the same declared desired state repeatedly, with no intervening changes, should always converge to a no-op after the first successful apply, not perform the underlying creation logic again or produce any side effect.

exercises.prompt: This provisioning script is meant to ensure exactly one 'worker' instance exists, and is run as a CI step that sometimes gets retried automatically after transient network failures. The team discovered duplicate worker instances after a retry happened. Find and fix the bug.
exercises.code:
#!/bin/bash
# provision-worker.sh
aws ec2 run-instances \
  --image-id ami-0abcdef1234567890 \
  --instance-type t3.micro \
  --tag-specifications 'ResourceType=instance,Tags=[{Key=Role,Value=worker}]' \
  --count 1
hints: Does this script check whether a worker instance already exists before creating a new one?

What happens if this exact script runs twice in a row -- for example because a CI retry re-executes the whole step after a network blip, with no way to know whether the first attempt actually succeeded?
Add a check beforehand: query for an existing instance tagged Role=worker, and only run `run-instances` if none is found.
exercises.solutionCode:
#!/bin/bash
# provision-worker.sh
EXISTING=$(aws ec2 describe-instances \
  --filters "Name=tag:Role,Values=worker" "Name=instance-state-name,Values=running,pending" \
  --query 'Reservations[].Instances[].InstanceId' --output text)

if [ -z "$EXISTING" ]; then
  aws ec2 run-instances \
    --image-id ami-0abcdef1234567890 \
    --instance-type t3.micro \
    --tag-specifications 'ResourceType=instance,Tags=[{Key=Role,Value=worker}]' \
    --count 1
else
  echo "Worker already exists ($EXISTING); skipping creation."
fi
exercises.solutionExplanation: The original script unconditionally calls `run-instances` every time it executes, with no notion of 'does a worker already exist' -- so a CI retry, which by definition re-runs the exact same step, creates a second worker instance identical in every way except its instance ID. The fix adds an explicit existence check via `describe-instances` filtered by the same tag the script itself sets, and only creates a new instance if none is found running or pending. This is exactly the kind of hand-written idempotency logic that a declarative tool like Terraform gives you automatically for every resource type -- which is the deeper lesson: imperative scripts *can* be made idempotent, but only by manually re-deriving, for every single resource, the same diff-and-reconcile behavior that declarative tooling provides as a first-class, built-in guarantee.

assessments.prompt: Why is idempotency specifically important for infrastructure automation that runs as a step inside a CI/CD pipeline?
options: Idempotent operations always execute faster than non-idempotent ones.

Pipelines routinely re-run the same step (retries after transient failures, re-runs of unrelated changes), and without idempotency, those re-runs risk creating duplicate or drifting resources instead of safely converging on the same target state.
Idempotency is a syntax requirement enforced by YAML-based pipeline configuration files.
It reduces cloud provider billing costs by definition.
assessments.explanation: The operational reason is about safety under repetition: pipeline steps get re-executed far more often than people expect, whether due to transient network retries, manually re-running a job, or scheduled reconciliation, and an idempotent apply guarantees those re-runs are safe no-ops when nothing has actually changed. Option A confuses idempotency (a correctness property about repeated execution) with performance, which isn't guaranteed either way. Option C is fabricated -- YAML syntax has nothing to do with idempotency. Option D might occasionally be a side effect of avoiding duplicate resources, but it isn't what idempotency means or guarantees.

assessments.prompt: A new engineer asks why the team insists nobody should use the cloud console to make manual changes to resources managed by Terraform, even for a 'quick fix.' Explain the reasoning.
assessments.modelAnswer: The moment a manual change is made outside the IaC tool, the resource's real-world state and the tool's recorded understanding of that state (and the declared configuration) start to disagree -- this is drift, and it begins immediately, regardless of any intention to reconcile it later. The specific danger of 'I'll update the .tf file afterward' is that it relies on a manual bookkeeping step happening under exactly the kind of time pressure (an urgent incident) that most reliably causes such steps to be forgotten. If it's forgotten, the very next ordinary `apply` -- run by anyone, possibly weeks later, with no idea an emergency fix ever happened -- can silently revert the fix, because from the tool's perspective the configuration never changed and reality has simply drifted back toward what it always specified. If the file does get updated but without an explanation, the next engineer who reads that value has no way to know it encodes a deliberate emergency decision rather than an arbitrary one. Beyond this specific failure mode, allowing manual exceptions at all erodes the broader guarantee that makes IaC trustworthy in the first place: that the code is the authoritative, complete description of what the infrastructure looks like, and that provenance is exactly what lets a team confidently review, audit, and reason about infrastructure changes the same way they do application code. The recommended process, even under real time pressure, is to make the emergency change through the IaC tool itself via a fast, targeted, reviewed apply, or to immediately follow up with a plan/apply cycle to consciously reconcile state before the drift has a chance to be forgotten.

concepts.title: Monitoring, Logging, and Alerting
concepts.description: Metrics, logs, and alerts are three distinct instruments for understanding a running system -- mixing up their roles, such as alerting on the wrong signal or logging what should be a metric, is what produces both noisy on-call rotations and blind spots during real incidents.
learningObjectives: Distinguish metrics and logs as different telemetry types, and explain what kind of question each is best suited to answer.
Explain why aggregated numeric metrics scale to high-traffic systems in a way that storing every raw log line doesn't.
Design an alert that is actionable and tied to user-facing impact rather than an internal implementation detail.
Explain alert fatigue and why paging on every anomaly degrades on-call responsiveness over time.
Distinguish symptom-based alerting from cause-based alerting, and explain why symptom-based alerts are generally preferred as the primary page.

sections.heading: Metrics: Cheap, Aggregated, Good for 'How Much' and 'How Many'
sections.body: Metrics are numeric time series -- counters, gauges, histograms -- sampled or aggregated over time: request count, error rate, p99 latency, CPU usage, queue depth. Their defining practical advantage is cost at scale: incrementing a counter costs the same small handful of bytes whether the underlying system is handling ten requests a day or ten million, because what's being stored is an aggregated number, not one record per individual event. This is exactly what makes metrics well-suited to dashboards, trend detection over long time windows, and alert thresholds ('page if error rate exceeds 1% for five minutes') -- they answer 'how much' and 'how many' extremely efficiently, at any scale.

sections.heading: Logs: Expensive, Granular, Good for 'What Exactly Happened'
sections.body:
Logs are discrete, timestamped event records carrying arbitrary detail -- a single request's full context: user id, request path, the exact stack trace on an error. The trade-off is the mirror image of metrics: storing a log line per event scales linearly with traffic, which gets genuinely expensive and slow to search at high volume, which is why teams sample verbose logs, index selectively, or set retention windows rather than keeping everything forever.

**Structured logging** -- emitting logs as fields in a consistent, machine-parseable shape (JSON, for example) rather than freeform sentences -- is what makes logs actually queryable at scale, letting you filter and aggregate by exact field values instead of relying on fragile string matching or regular expressions. The core distinction from metrics is what question each answers: a metric can tell you the error rate spiked at 3:02pm, but to see the actual stack trace and specific request context behind even one of those failures, you need a log line -- metrics tell you *that* something happened and roughly how much; logs tell you *what exactly* happened for one specific instance of it.

sections.heading: Alerting: Turning Signals Into Action
sections.body:
Alerting is the layer that watches signals -- usually metrics -- against a condition, and notifies a human (sometimes waking them up) when that condition is met. The central design tension is calibration: thresholds set too sensitively create **alert fatigue** -- frequent pages for things that turn out not to matter, which trains on-call responders to treat pages as noise to dismiss or snooze, a habit that becomes dangerous precisely at the moment a real incident finally does happen. Thresholds set too loosely mean genuine incidents go unnoticed until a customer reports them, which is far worse.

A practical way to manage this tension is tiering: not every abnormal signal deserves to wake someone up. A condition that's urgent and requires immediate human action should page; a condition that's worth investigating but isn't urgent should become a ticket; a condition that's just useful context should live on a dashboard, visible but silent. Treating every anomaly as page-worthy collapses this useful hierarchy and is one of the most common causes of on-call burnout.

sections.heading: Symptom-Based vs Cause-Based Alerting
sections.body:
**Symptom-based** alerts fire on user-facing impact -- error rate as experienced by users, latency against an agreed SLO. **Cause-based** alerts fire on an internal condition that *might* lead to impact -- CPU at 90%, a specific pod restarting, disk queue depth climbing.

Symptom-based alerts are generally preferred as the primary page for three concrete reasons: they directly reflect what actually matters (is a user experiencing a problem, right now); they're robust to internal architecture changes (adding a new internal component doesn't require a new alert unless it actually produces user-visible impact); and they avoid paging for internal conditions that turn out to be harmless (CPU spiked during a nightly batch job, but nobody noticed anything and nothing broke). This doesn't make cause-based signals worthless -- they remain genuinely valuable as diagnostic dashboards and as lower-urgency tickets for proactive investigation before a cause-based condition ever escalates into a real symptom -- they're simply usually the wrong signal to wake someone up over at 3am on their own.

sections.heading: Common Mistakes: Noisy Logs, Metric-Shaped Logs, and Vanity Dashboards
sections.body: A few recurring anti-patterns are worth naming explicitly. First, logging so verbosely that the signal drowns in noise -- emitting an INFO-level line for every single request on a high-traffic service buries the rare, important ERROR lines under a flood of routine ones, making both manual investigation and automated log-based alerting harder rather than easier. Second, using logs to answer a question metrics should answer -- counting matching log lines to approximate a rate is slower, more expensive, and less accurate than simply incrementing a counter directly in the code at the moment the event happens; if you find yourself grepping logs to compute something that sounds like a rate or a count, that's usually a sign a metric is missing, not that logs need to be searched harder. Third, building dashboards that nobody actually looks at until an incident is already underway -- a dashboard that only gets opened reactively isn't doing the proactive watching that alerting exists for; if a condition is important enough to want a dashboard for, it's worth asking whether it's also important enough to have an actual alert on.

examples.title: A Metric vs a Log Line for the Same Event
examples.explanation: `metrics.increment("payments.failure")` gives a cheap, aggregable number that can be graphed over time and used directly as an alert condition ('page if payments.failure rate exceeds 2% over 5 minutes') -- it answers 'how much is failing, and when.' The structured `logger.error` call gives the specific context needed to actually debug one particular failed payment once an alert has told you something is wrong -- which order, what amount, what the underlying error actually was. Neither one is redundant with the other: the metric is what should trigger the page, and the log line is what an engineer opens next to find out exactly what happened for a specific instance of the problem the metric already told them exists.

examples.title: A Well-Designed Symptom-Based Alert vs a Noisy Cause-Based One
examples.code:
groups:
  - name: symptom-based
    rules:
      - alert: HighCheckoutErrorRate
        expr: rate(http_requests_total{route="/checkout", status=~"5.."}[5m])
              / rate(http_requests_total{route="/checkout"}[5m]) > 0.01
        for: 5m
        labels: { severity: page }

  - name: cause-based
    rules:
      - alert: HighCPU
        expr: cpu_usage_percent > 90
        for: 1m
        labels: { severity: ticket }   # deliberately NOT severity: page
examples.explanation: `HighCheckoutErrorRate` is symptom-based -- it measures actual user-facing failure on a specific, important route, and is deliberately tagged to page, since a sustained error rate above 1% on checkout is a real, immediate user-impacting problem. `HighCPU` is cause-based -- CPU alone says nothing about whether users are actually experiencing any problem, and it's deliberately tagged `severity: ticket` rather than `severity: page`, precisely because a CPU spike (say, from a nightly batch job) with no accompanying symptom shouldn't wake anyone up. Note also the `for: 5m` on the symptom alert versus `for: 1m` on the cause alert -- the symptom alert requires the condition to persist for five minutes before firing, filtering out brief, self-resolving blips that would otherwise generate a page for a problem that was already gone by the time anyone looked at it.

examples.title: Structured Logging for Queryability
examples.explanation: Because every field is a named, consistently-typed key rather than free text embedded in a sentence, a log platform can run an exact query like 'all logs where status=500 AND route=/checkout AND error=card_declined' directly against indexed fields. The freeform equivalent -- something like `logger.error(f"Payment failed for order {order_id}: card_declined")` -- requires fragile regex or substring matching to answer the same question, and any small change in the sentence's wording (a typo, a rephrase during a later refactor) silently breaks whatever search or alert was built against that specific text pattern. Structured fields don't just make a single lookup easier -- they're what makes aggregation across many log lines (counting, grouping by field) tractable at all.

misconceptions.description: If something might indicate a problem, like CPU usage climbing, it should page someone immediately so they can look into it right away.
misconceptions.clarification: Cause-based signals like CPU usage are frequently harmless, self-resolving, or simply correlated with legitimate load (a scheduled batch job, a traffic spike that the system handles fine) -- paging on every such internal fluctuation, with no confirmation of actual user impact, is exactly what produces alert fatigue: on-call responders learn that pages are frequently not urgent, and that learned habit degrades their response to the pages that actually matter. The better model reserves paging for symptom-based, user-impact-confirmed conditions, and routes cause-based signals to dashboards or lower-urgency tickets, where they remain genuinely useful for proactive investigation without demanding an interrupt-driven, right-now response.

misconceptions.description: Logging everything at high verbosity is strictly safer than logging too little, since you can always filter down later.
misconceptions.clarification: Extremely verbose logging has real, compounding costs: storage and ingestion cost that scales roughly linearly with traffic, and -- more importantly for actually finding problems -- it buries the rare, genuinely important lines (errors, warnings) inside a flood of routine ones, making both manual investigation and log-based alerting harder rather than easier, since 'filtering down later' still requires the important lines to be findable and distinguishable from noise in the first place. The better approach is deliberate log-level discipline (being honest about what's genuinely INFO versus DEBUG versus ERROR) combined with structured fields, which lets you filter effectively by design rather than hoping you logged 'everything, just in case' and can somehow find the needle later.

exercises.prompt: You're instrumenting a checkout service's card-charging call. Write the instrumentation (pseudocode is fine) so that (a) you could build a dashboard and alert on the overall charge failure rate, and (b) you could look up exactly what happened for one specific failed charge given its order id.
exercises.code:
def charge_card(order_id, amount, card_token):
    # TODO: add instrumentation for both (a) an aggregable failure-rate signal
    # and (b) a way to look up full context for one specific failure
    result = payment_gateway.charge(card_token, amount)
    return result
hints: These are two different needs requiring two different kinds of telemetry -- don't try to satisfy both with just one of them.
For (a), think about what you'd actually want to graph and set a threshold-based alert on -- a count/rate is exactly what a metric is built for.
For (b), think about what an engineer would need in front of them to diagnose one specific failed order -- that calls for a structured log line carrying the order id and the actual error detail.
exercises.solutionExplanation: `metrics.increment` on both the success and failure path gives an aggregable pair of counters that a dashboard can turn into a failure rate over time, and that an alert can threshold against ('page if failure rate exceeds X% over 5 minutes') -- this satisfies (a) without needing to touch a single log line. The structured `logger.error` call, tagged with `order_id` and the actual error detail, is what satisfies (b): once an alert (built on the metric) tells you something is wrong in aggregate, you can query logs filtered to a specific `order_id` a customer reported and see exactly what error occurred for that one charge. Neither piece of instrumentation could substitute for the other -- the metric can't tell you what went wrong for one specific order, and grepping/counting log lines to approximate a failure rate would be slower, costlier, and less precise than a purpose-built counter.

exercises.prompt: This alert pages on-call for every single ERROR-level log line, and the team is being paged constantly, including for single, isolated, already-retried transient errors that had no real user impact. Find and fix the underlying problem with the alert.
exercises.code:
groups:
  - name: errors
    rules:
      - alert: AnyErrorLogged
        expr: count(log_lines{level="error"}) > 0
        for: 0s
        labels: { severity: page }
hints: This alert fires the instant a single ERROR log line exists at all -- does that actually mean users are experiencing a sustained, meaningful problem?

Compare this to a rate-based, user-impact-based condition -- what would it look like to alert on the *proportion* of failing requests sustained over a *window of time*, instead of the mere existence of any one error line?
Rewrite the expression to compute an error rate over a time window, require it to exceed a meaningful threshold, and require it to persist for a few minutes (via `for:`) before paging.
exercises.solutionCode:
groups:
  - name: errors
    rules:
      - alert: SustainedElevatedErrorRate
        expr: rate(http_requests_total{status=~"5.."}[5m])
              / rate(http_requests_total[5m]) > 0.01
        for: 5m
        labels: { severity: page }
exercises.solutionExplanation: The original alert conflates 'an error happened at all, even once' with 'there is a real, ongoing, user-impacting problem' -- a single isolated error (a request that failed once and was successfully retried, with zero visible impact) trips it exactly as readily as a genuine sustained outage, which is precisely why it pages constantly for things that don't matter. This is a textbook cause of alert fatigue: after enough false-alarm pages, on-call responders start treating this alert as noise, which is dangerous the one time it actually does correspond to something serious. The fix reframes the condition as a symptom-based, rate-over-time signal: the proportion of failing requests over a 5-minute window, required to exceed a meaningful threshold (1%, here) and to persist for 5 minutes (`for: 5m`) before actually paging -- which naturally filters out brief, isolated, self-resolving errors while still catching genuinely sustained problems.

assessments.prompt: A service's CPU usage spikes to 95% for 90 seconds during a nightly batch job, then returns to normal, with no user-facing errors or latency increase observed during or after. What is the most appropriate response for the team's alerting setup?
options: Page on-call immediately so someone can investigate the spike in real time.
This shouldn't page on-call directly, since there's no confirmed user-facing symptom -- but it's reasonable to have it visible on a dashboard, or filed as a low-urgency ticket for later review.
Ignore it entirely and remove CPU monitoring from the system altogether.
Log the CPU value at ERROR level from within the application code.
assessments.explanation: With no confirmed user-facing impact, paging (option A) is a textbook alert-fatigue-generating decision -- it interrupts a human for a condition that, in this case, correlates with expected, harmless load. Cause-based signals like CPU still have real diagnostic value, though, so removing monitoring entirely (option C) throws away information that could matter in a different scenario (for example, if a similar spike ever did correlate with degraded latency). Option D conflates an application log (meant for discrete events with rich context) with an infrastructure metric time series, which is the wrong tool for tracking a continuously varying numeric signal like CPU usage. The correct middle ground -- visible but not paging -- reflects that this is a cause-based signal worth watching, not a confirmed symptom worth interrupting someone over.

assessments.prompt: Explain the difference between symptom-based and cause-based alerting, and why most teams prefer symptom-based alerts as their primary page.
assessments.modelAnswer: Symptom-based alerts fire on directly user-facing impact -- error rate as experienced by real requests, latency measured against an agreed service-level objective -- while cause-based alerts fire on an internal condition, like CPU usage or disk queue depth, that might eventually lead to user-facing impact but doesn't necessarily mean it has. Symptom-based alerts are generally preferred as the primary page for a few concrete reasons. First, they directly reflect what actually matters to the business and to users: whether someone is experiencing a real problem right now, rather than whether some internal number crossed an arbitrary threshold that may or may not correlate with any real consequence. Second, they're robust to internal architectural change -- adding, removing, or refactoring an internal component doesn't require inventing a new cause-based alert for it unless that change actually produces user-visible impact, whereas a purely cause-based alerting strategy tends to require constant upkeep as internals evolve. Third, and most concretely, cause-based conditions are frequently harmless: a CPU spike during an expected nightly batch job, or a brief queue depth increase that drains on its own, will trip a cause-based alert with no accompanying symptom, and paging on that kind of noise is exactly what produces alert fatigue -- on-call responders learn, correctly, that many pages don't correspond to anything requiring urgent action, and that learned skepticism inevitably bleeds into how they react to the pages that do matter. None of this makes cause-based signals worthless; they remain genuinely useful as diagnostic dashboards and as lower-urgency tickets for proactive investigation before a cause-based condition escalates into an actual symptom. The point is narrower: they're usually the wrong signal to wake a specific human up over at 3am, and symptom-based signals -- because they measure the thing that actually matters -- are the better default choice for that specific, highest-urgency role.

concepts.title: Observability vs. Monitoring, and Postmortem Thinking
concepts.description: Monitoring tells you whether known failure modes are happening; observability is the ability to ask new questions about a system's internal state from its external outputs without shipping new code to answer them -- and a blameless postmortem is how a team turns one specific outage into a durable systemic improvement in both, rather than just a scar and a grudge.
learningObjectives: Explain the difference between monitoring (watching for known failure conditions) and observability (the capacity to investigate unknown or novel failure conditions after the fact).
Explain why high-cardinality, high-dimensionality telemetry is what enables true observability, as opposed to pre-aggregated dashboards.
Describe the role of distributed tracing in diagnosing latency and failure issues across service boundaries that logs and metrics alone can't localize.
Explain the purpose and structure of a blameless postmortem, and why blame-seeking postmortems tend to produce worse long-term outcomes.
Write or evaluate a postmortem's timeline and action items for an incident, and judge whether those action items are concrete, owned, and systemic.

sections.heading: Monitoring: Answering Questions You Already Thought to Ask
sections.body: Monitoring means watching a predetermined set of known signals -- dashboards and alerts built in advance -- for known failure modes: 'is error rate above X,' 'is disk almost full,' 'is p99 latency creeping up.' It is, by its very nature, retrospective in scope: a team can only monitor for problems that someone anticipated clearly enough, ahead of time, to build a specific metric, dashboard panel, or alert rule for. That's not a criticism of monitoring -- it's genuinely necessary, and it catches the large majority of day-to-day operational problems efficiently and cheaply. But it structurally cannot cover the failure modes nobody thought to ask about in advance -- the 'unknown unknowns' -- because there's no dashboard for a question nobody knew to ask.

sections.heading: Observability: Answering Questions You Didn't Know You'd Need to Ask
sections.body:
Observability, borrowing loosely from its control-theory origins (can you infer a system's internal state purely from its external outputs), is the capacity to explore and debug a genuinely novel failure *after the fact*, without having to ship new instrumentation specifically to catch that one new question. It's enabled by rich, high-cardinality, high-dimensionality event data -- for example, every request recorded as a structured event carrying dozens of fields: user id, region, which feature flags were active, exact code path taken, a timing breakdown -- that can be sliced and filtered along dimensions nobody thought to pre-aggregate into a dashboard ahead of time.

The contrast with a dashboard is precise: a dashboard pre-aggregates along dimensions chosen in advance, such as error rate broken down by region. If the actual novel bug turns out to be 'errors only occur for users with a specific, rare combination of two feature flags enabled, and only on an outdated app version,' a by-region dashboard built last quarter simply cannot reveal that -- the dimension that matters was never one of the ones it aggregates along. An observability tool that retains raw, high-cardinality event data lets an engineer construct that exact, previously-unplanned filter on the fly, after the incident is already underway, which is precisely the capability a fixed set of pre-built dashboards cannot offer no matter how many of them exist.

sections.heading: Distributed Tracing: Localizing Failure Across Service Boundaries
sections.body:
A **trace** follows a single request as it crosses multiple services -- an API gateway, then an auth service, then an order service, then a payment service -- recording a **span** per hop, each with its own timing and metadata, all connected by a shared trace id and parent-child span relationships. This matters enormously in a distributed, microservices-style architecture specifically because a slow user-facing request could be slow due to any one of several downstream calls, and metrics or logs scoped to any single service can each look individually healthy while the request as a whole is still slow -- only a trace shows the request's full path and reveals exactly which hop actually consumed the time.

```text
[api-gateway         ] 0ms -------- 420ms
  [auth-service       ] 5ms --- 45ms
  [order-service      ] 50ms ---------------- 400ms
    [payment-service  ] 60ms ------------------------- 395ms
      [db-query        ] 65ms ---------------------------- 390ms
```

Each indented span is nested in time inside its caller's span, and the widths make the bottleneck visually obvious: the vast majority of this request's 420ms total is consumed inside one `db-query` span, deeply nested inside `payment-service` -- not spread evenly across the five services involved. Without the trace, an on-call engineer might check `payment-service`'s own dashboards, see nothing obviously wrong at the service level (average latency there might look fine across all its other queries), and have no principled way to know that this *specific* request's slowness traces down to one particular query, rather than guessing across every service in the request path.

sections.heading: Blameless Postmortems: The Point Is the System, Not the Person
sections.body:
After an incident, a postmortem produces a factual timeline, the incident's contributing factors (almost always plural -- real incidents are rarely caused by exactly one thing), and concrete action items -- explicitly without assigning individual blame. This isn't merely a kindness; it produces measurably better long-term outcomes than a blame-seeking alternative. If postmortems are used to identify who to blame, people respond entirely rationally by hiding information, hedging their account of events, or simply avoiding being the person who touches risky systems or makes the next deploy -- all of which starves the *next* postmortem of the honest, detailed account it needs to actually find the real contributing factors, and discourages exactly the kind of ownership and calculated risk-taking that keeps systems evolving and improving.

The reframing that makes this work in practice: 'human error' is treated as a *symptom* of a system that made the error easy to make -- a missing safeguard, a confusing interface, an absent or outdated runbook, an alert that should have fired but didn't -- rather than as the root cause itself. 'So-and-so made a mistake' isn't something you can fix going forward, because the same mistake remains exactly as easy for the next person (or the same person, on a worse day) to make. 'Why was it possible, even easy, for a reasonable and well-intentioned engineer to make this specific mistake' is an actionable systems question with a real, buildable answer.

sections.heading: Anatomy of a Postmortem: Timeline, Contributing Factors, Action Items
sections.body:
A useful postmortem has a consistent shape: an incident summary (what happened, user impact, duration); a detailed timeline with real timestamps (detection, escalation, mitigation, resolution -- these timestamps are themselves worth tracking as metrics across incidents over time, not just within one write-up); contributing factors, described systemically and in the plural rather than pinned on a person; and action items that are concrete, explicitly owned by a specific named person, and tracked to completion -- a postmortem whose action items quietly never get done is theater, not process improvement.

One specific, high-leverage habit is separating **time-to-detect** from **time-to-mitigate** within the timeline. A long time-to-detect points toward an observability or alerting gap -- the problem existed and was impacting users well before anyone or anything noticed, which argues for better symptom-based alerting or richer telemetry. A long time-to-mitigate, once the problem was already known, points toward a different kind of gap entirely -- missing runbooks, slow or manual rollback tooling, unclear on-call ownership -- which argues for investing in faster, more mechanical recovery paths (echoing the deploy-stage design covered earlier in this subject) rather than better detection. Conflating the two in a single 'time to resolve' number obscures which of these two very different problems actually needs fixing.

examples.title: A Question a Dashboard Can't Answer, But an Observability Query Can
examples.code:
SELECT count(*) FROM requests
WHERE feature_flag_new_checkout = true
  AND app_version < '4.2.0'
  AND region = 'eu-west-1'
  AND status >= 500;
examples.explanation: This is an ad hoc, previously unplanned combination of dimensions, constructed *after* an incident began, to chase a specific emerging hypothesis -- and it's only answerable at all because every request was recorded as a rich structured event carrying all of these fields (feature flag state, app version, region, status) individually. No dashboard built in advance would have happened to pre-aggregate exactly this particular intersection of four dimensions, because nobody knew to ask this specific question until the incident was already underway and this hypothesis had formed. This is the concrete difference between monitoring (which requires the question to have been anticipated) and observability (which lets the question be constructed on the fly, from raw enough data to support whatever it turns out to be).

examples.title: A Trace Waterfall Revealing the Real Bottleneck
examples.explanation: Reading the indentation as call nesting and the dashes as elapsed time, it's immediately visible that `auth-service` finishes quickly (40ms) and contributes little to the total, while the request spends the overwhelming majority of its 420ms total deep inside a single `db-query` span nested inside `payment-service`. Without this trace, an engineer investigating slowness would have to check each of five services' own dashboards individually, and each one might report perfectly normal *average* latency across all the requests it handles -- because this slow query could be a rare outlier drowned out in an average. The trace localizes the problem to one specific hop for one specific request, turning 'something somewhere is slow' into 'this exact query, in this exact service, is the thing to investigate' -- likely pointing toward a missing index, lock contention, or an N+1 query pattern, rather than a vague, system-wide performance mystery.

examples.title: A Blameless vs Blame-Seeking Postmortem Excerpt
examples.code:
BLAME-SEEKING:
"Alex deployed a bad config and caused the outage. Alex should be more careful
with config changes going forward."

BLAMELESS:
"A configuration change that removed a required field was deployed without a
schema-validation step catching it pre-deploy. The on-call engineer who approved
the deploy had no automated signal indicating that field was required by a
downstream service. Action items: (1) add schema validation to the config
deploy pipeline [owner: Priya, due Aug 21], (2) add a pre-deploy check that
flags removed fields referenced by other services [owner: Priya, due Aug 28]."
examples.explanation: The blame-seeking version identifies a person and a vague, unenforceable intention ('be more careful') that has no way to be verified as done, and, worse, does absolutely nothing to change how likely the same mistake is for literally anyone else who deploys a config change tomorrow -- the missing safeguard is still missing. The blameless version identifies two specific, fixable system gaps -- no schema validation, no cross-service dependency check -- and pairs each with a named owner and a concrete due date, which is both verifiable (did Priya's PR merge by the 21st, yes or no) and genuinely preventive, because it closes the gap that made the mistake easy for anyone to make, not just for Alex specifically. Notice, too, that the blameless version can only exist if Alex (and whoever approved the deploy) was willing to describe honestly what happened and why it seemed reasonable at the time -- exactly the kind of candor that a blame-seeking postmortem culture actively discourages.

misconceptions.description: Observability is just a fancier, rebranded word for monitoring -- if you have dashboards and alerts, you're doing observability.
misconceptions.clarification: The real distinction is about what class of question your telemetry is capable of answering, not about how much of it you have or how good it looks. Monitoring answers pre-anticipated questions via dashboards and alerts built ahead of time on aggregated, typically lower-cardinality data. Observability is specifically the ability to construct and answer genuinely new questions after the fact, about failure modes nobody anticipated, using rich, raw, high-cardinality event or trace data. A system can have excellent dashboards -- genuinely strong monitoring -- and still be poorly observable, if that pre-aggregated data is all that's retained, because the specific combination of fields needed to answer an unplanned question was thrown away (or never captured) before anyone had a chance to ask it.

misconceptions.description: The goal of a postmortem is to figure out who made the mistake, so it doesn't happen again.
misconceptions.clarification: Identifying an individual doesn't actually prevent recurrence, because the underlying system condition that made the mistake easy to make is still there, equally ready to let the next person -- or the same person, on a different day -- make the same or a similar mistake. The actual goal is to identify the systemic contributing factors (a missing safeguard, an absent validation step, an unclear runbook, an alerting gap) that let a reasonable, well-intentioned engineer's honest action turn into an incident, and to fix those factors specifically, since that is what generalizes to prevent similar incidents regardless of who happens to be involved next time.

exercises.prompt: Given this incident summary, write the three or four highest-value postmortem action items you'd propose. Each item should be concrete enough that anyone could later check, unambiguously, whether it was actually done -- and each should target a systemic gap, not an individual's behavior.
exercises.code:
Incident summary: A deploy removed a database column that an older, still-running
version of a downstream reporting service depended on. The reporting service began
erroring on every report generation. It took 40 minutes to detect (no alert fired;
a customer reported broken reports) and 10 minutes to mitigate once detected (a
known, fast rollback script was run immediately).
hints: Separate the two very different timeline problems here: a 40-minute time-to-detect versus a 10-minute time-to-mitigate. What kind of gap does each one point toward, and are they the same kind of fix?
The 10-minute mitigation was fast specifically because a rollback script already existed and was known -- that's worth noting as something that worked, not just something to fix.
For the 40-minute detection gap: what alert or check, if it had existed beforehand, would have caught 'a downstream service started erroring on every request' well before a customer had to report it?
exercises.solutionCode:
1. Add a symptom-based alert on the reporting service's error rate (e.g. page if
   error rate exceeds 5% for 5 minutes) so incidents like this are detected
   automatically rather than via customer report. [owner: on-call lead, due in 1 week]

2. Add a pre-deploy check in the migration pipeline that flags any column being
   dropped or renamed if it is still referenced by another service's schema or
   query, blocking the deploy until that dependency is resolved or the downstream
   service is confirmed updated first. [owner: platform team, due in 2 weeks]

3. Document and formally adopt the expand-contract migration pattern for any
   schema change with a downstream consumer, so old and new versions can both
   run correctly during a rollout window instead of an old version breaking
   immediately. [owner: platform team, due in 2 weeks]

4. (Note, not an action item): the 10-minute mitigation was fast specifically
   because a known rollback script already existed -- preserve and keep testing
   that script as part of future related changes.
exercises.solutionExplanation: Item 1 targets the 40-minute detection gap specifically -- a symptom-based alert (error rate, tied to real user/consumer impact) would have caught this automatically, likely within minutes, rather than waiting on a customer to notice and report it. Items 2 and 3 target the actual root contributing factor rather than 'the engineer who dropped the column should have checked first' -- they close the gap systemically, for every future schema change made by anyone, not just for this one incident. Note the deliberate absence of anything like 'remind engineers to check downstream dependencies before dropping columns' -- that kind of item isn't verifiable (there's no way to check later whether anyone was successfully 'reminded') and doesn't change how easy the mistake still is to make; a required automated check does both. The closing note about the rollback script is included because a good postmortem also explicitly calls out what worked well, not only what needs fixing -- the fast mitigation was itself the product of earlier, deliberate investment worth reinforcing rather than treating as unremarkable luck.

exercises.prompt: This postmortem excerpt has real problems with both its framing and its action items. Identify what's wrong and rewrite it.
exercises.code:
Root cause: Jordan pushed a config change on a Friday afternoon without testing
it properly.

Action items:
- Jordan should test changes more thoroughly before deploying.
- Team should be more careful with Friday deploys.
hints: Look at who and what this excerpt names as the 'root cause' -- is a person's specific behavior actually a fixable root cause, or is it a symptom of something else that made this easy to get wrong?
For each action item, ask: could someone, three months from now, check objectively whether this was actually done? What would 'more careful' or 'more thoroughly' even look like as a pass/fail check?

Rewrite the root cause as a systemic gap (what safeguard was missing that would have caught this regardless of who deployed it, or on what day), and rewrite each action item as something concrete, owned, and verifiable.
exercises.solutionCode:
Root cause: The config deploy pipeline had no automated validation step, so a
config error that a schema check would have caught instead reached production
undetected. No policy or automated gate distinguished Friday-afternoon deploys
from any other time, despite the team's reduced on-call staffing on Fridays.

Action items:
- Add automated schema validation to the config deploy pipeline, blocking any
  deploy that fails it. [owner: Priya, due in 1 week]
- Add a pipeline check that requires explicit senior on-call sign-off for any
  deploy initiated after 2pm on a Friday, rather than relying on informal
  team norms. [owner: release engineering, due in 2 weeks]
exercises.solutionExplanation: The original excerpt names a person and a vague personal quality ('more careful,' 'more thoroughly') as both the root cause and the fix -- neither is actionable, since there's no way to verify 'being more careful' happened, and neither one makes the same mistake any harder for Jordan (on a worse day) or anyone else to make again next time. The rewrite identifies the actual systemic gaps: no automated schema validation existed, and no real gate (as opposed to an informal norm) governed risky-timing deploys. Each rewritten action item names a specific, verifiable deliverable with a named owner and a due date -- 'was schema validation added to the pipeline, yes or no' is a fact that can be checked later, unlike 'was Jordan more careful.' This is also why the rewrite doesn't mention Jordan by name at all: the fix targets the conditions that made the mistake easy, which is exactly what prevents the next person -- not just Jordan -- from hitting the same gap.

assessments.prompt: A team has strong dashboards for CPU, memory, request rate, and error rate broken down by service. During a real incident, none of these dashboards show anything unusual, yet a specific subset of users is clearly experiencing failures. What does this scenario best illustrate?
options: The team has strong monitoring but limited observability, since their existing telemetry is pre-aggregated along dimensions that don't happen to isolate this particular failure mode.
The dashboards are useless and should be deleted entirely.
The team should immediately page a larger number of people until someone notices the cause.
The incident isn't actually real, since the dashboards show no problem.
assessments.explanation: This is precisely the gap between monitoring and observability described in the concept: pre-built dashboards aggregate along dimensions chosen in advance (service, region, and so on), and if the real failure mode cuts across some other combination of dimensions nobody anticipated, those dashboards can look entirely healthy while a real, specific problem is happening. Option B overreacts -- the dashboards remain useful for the failure modes they were built to catch; they're simply insufficient for this one. Option C treats headcount as a substitute for the right telemetry, which doesn't address the actual gap. Option D wrongly treats dashboard silence as proof no problem exists, which is exactly the mistaken inference this scenario is meant to correct.

assessments.prompt: A teammate proposes writing a postmortem that names the specific engineer who wrote the buggy code, arguing that transparency about who did what is important. Explain why this is generally considered bad postmortem practice, and what to do instead.
assessments.modelAnswer: The problem isn't transparency itself -- a good postmortem should be honest and specific about what actually happened -- it's specifically attaching blame to an individual as if that were the actionable finding. Naming an engineer as the cause doesn't change how easy the underlying mistake still is to make; whatever missing safeguard, confusing tooling, or absent validation step let a reasonable, well-intentioned person's honest action turn into an incident is still there afterward, equally ready to let the next person (or that same person on a different day) make the same or a similar mistake. Worse, making postmortems about identifying who to blame has a real chilling effect on future postmortems: people who expect to be blamed respond rationally by hiding detail, softening their account of what happened, or avoiding the riskier work altogether, which starves the next investigation of exactly the honest, granular account it needs to find the real systemic contributing factors. What to do instead is treat 'a person wrote buggy code' as a symptom rather than a root cause, and ask the more useful question underneath it: why was it possible, or even easy, for a reasonable engineer to write and ship this bug -- was there no test covering this case, no code review catching it, no schema validation, no staging environment that would have surfaced it? Each of those is a concrete, fixable system gap that, once closed, reduces the chance of a similar bug from anyone, not just the one engineer involved this time -- which is both the more effective fix and the one that keeps the postmortem process itself trustworthy enough that people keep being honest in it.
